claims.text: Electrochemical pre-treatment can shift the balance between metallic and partially oxidized catalyst sites.
Changing the metallic-to-partially-oxidized site balance will modulate ethanol oxidation performance.
The oxidation-state balance affects ethanol oxidation by changing adsorption and conversion of ethanol-derived intermediates.
Under steady-state fuel-cell-like ethanol oxidation conditions, the catalyst surface is predominantly metallic.
Under operating conditions, a minor fraction of oxidized PGM sites forms dynamically.
Potential pulsing can selectively increase or decrease the fraction of partially oxidized PGM sites.
The metallic-to-partially-oxidized site ratio can be monitored in real time using in situ XAS or Raman spectroscopy.
A higher fraction of partially oxidized sites changes the binding energies of key ethanol oxidation intermediates.
The altered intermediate binding facilitates more efficient 12-electron and 12-proton ethanol oxidation.
More efficient transfer of the required electrons and protons improves catalytic activity and product selectivity.
Either too much or too little surface oxidation can adversely affect catalyst durability.
Increasing the proportion of partially oxidized sites should enhance ethanol oxidation rate relative to an untreated catalyst.
Increasing the proportion of partially oxidized sites should improve ethanol oxidation product selectivity relative to an untreated catalyst.
Extreme oxidation-state shifts in either direction may cause degradation or suboptimal catalytic performance.
The proposed oxidation-state mechanism applies within the normal fuel-cell operating potential window.
Potentials substantially outside the normal operating window may cause irreversible structural changes or degradation that break the oxidation-state/performance relationship.
